Karoo Uranium

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Despite a flatlining world uranium price, Australian miner Peninsula, backed by Russian capital, angles to mine uranium in the Karoo, threatening precious water sources.

Summary:
Very nearly too late, experts and affected parties -- like the vulnerable farmers of the Karoo, heard that Peninsula Energy and its local partners have been planning to mine 750,000ha of the water-scarce, ecologically sensitive region.
But by mid-year, Karoo-based Dr Stefan Cramer, science advisor to the Southern African Faith Communities' Environment Initiative (SAFCEI is taking government to court for its secretive handling of the new nuclear build programme) had rallied massive support of communities in the region to make their voices heard against the company's plans to use up and pollute major water sources in its quest for uranium profits.
Now the company has pulled back on its original plan, reducing their application to only 70,000ha.
What made them do this?
Was the the rising tide of activism against their now slowing dawning plans?
Was the the astute analysis of their ostensibly self-serving environmental impact assessments by provincial environmental departments and organised agriculture?
Does the reduction in the territory make any difference to the amount of water that will be lost now and in the generations to come -- as uranium and its toxic decay products linger in the environment for geological ages to come.

Further information:
Peninsula's full proposal can be viewed here: https://www.dropbox.com/s/kbd0zibgrmoch14/Update%20to%20IAP%20-%206%20July%202016.pdf?dl=0

Activists believe that it was constructive and measured criticism by the Karoo people and civil society of the pending mining rights application that forced the company to reduce its mining rights footprint to 12 % of their original intention. They believe the company pre-empted an outright rejection of the application by the Department of Mineral Resources. That is why even the vastly reduced application has to be done from scratch.

While this is a victory in the short term, the fact remains that it would seem the company is working to elbow out any competition in the region by holding out promises for jobs, to position themselves for a new nuclear future in the country.

Meanwhile, ahead of local government elections, the ANC mayor for Beaufort West, Truman Prince, has said that he has many plans to put the small Karoo town on the global map, including plans for fracking and large-scale uranium mining. And he totally discounted any warnings about radiological water contamination.

Press Release:


Karoo Uranium Mining
The Karoo is under serious threat yet again. Against the backdrop of the worst droughts in living memory, farmers and activists who were once at the forefront of the fight against fracking, now face the looming spectre of uranium mining. At the same time, communities surrounding Beaufort West are desperate for the employment opportunities the mine may bring. Carte Blanche asks: could the radioactive dust from surface mining leave indelible scars on the health of residents, export wool production and this pristine landscape?



10 secs:
10 secs A proposed uranium mine in the heart of the sensitive Karoo – is it the cure-all for unemployment – or the worst threat to the environment to date?

15 secs:
UPS STEFAN CRAMER: We know from hundreds of studies that uranium mining has a terrible record…
9 secs The threat of fracking is still pending, and now there are plans to mine uranium in the Karoo – can the few jobs created be worth the possible long-term damage?

15 secs:
10 secs Could opencast uranium mining around Beaufort West threaten the water supply of a town already desperate for the scarce resource?
UPS CALLIE: If there’s a problem with the water supply, then we can shut down Beaufort-West.



Script:


KAROO URANIUM
18 secs: Midway between Joburg and Cape Town lies Beaufort West, capital of the Karoo and home to the famous Karoo lamb and mohair industries. A melting pot of emotive contrasts, the Karoo’s unique flora, fossils and farming belie chronic drought and joblessness.
JOHN LINK: The natural environment here in the Karoo is under threat on a number of fronts amidst one of the worst droughts in recent memory. Communities here have been at the forefront of the fight against fracking. Now the prospectors are back and the spectre of uranium mining looms large.
JAN BOSTANDER, FARMER AND AGRI CENTRAL KAROO CONSERVATION COMMITTEE MEMBER:  When I hear about the mine in our area and especially so close to me…it’s quite an unnerving thing.
DR CALLIE POTGIETER, BEAUFORT WEST DENTIST: If there’s a problem with the water supply, then we can shut down Beaufort-West.
25 secs: Abundant uranium deposits across the Karoo have attracted the latest in a series of mining hopefuls – Australian-listed Peninsula Energy. Last month the local directors, who call their consortium TASMAN RSA, presented their plans for an open-cast mine that will employ 1000 people during construction, and 250 when operational, to Beaufort-West’s residents.
WILLIE BEZUIDENHOUT, CEO, TASMAN RSA MINES: Tasman remains committed to the development of its assets in Beaufort West and surrounding areas. We’re committed to doing that responsibly, not only for the benefit of our shareholders but also for the benefit of the community of Beaufort West and surrounding areas.
15 secs: Willie Bezuidenhout was appointed CEO in June. This followed months of bad press after locals discovered Tasman was applying to mine a massive area spanning three provinces: the Western, Northern and Eastern Cape.
JOHN LINK: The original mining application was for 750 000 hectares. That’s an area that can be seen from out of space. But after a public outcry and a number of critical submissions, that area was reduced to 75 000 hectares.
11.5 secs: Tasman is planning so-called ‘conventional acid leach mining’ and says uranium ore going to their mill will be kept wet to minimise uranium dust impact. But concerns remain.
DR STEFAN CRAMER, SCIENCE ADVISER, SOUTH AFRICAN FAITH COMMUNITIES’ ENVIRONMENTAL INITIATIVE: We know from hundreds of studies that uranium mining has a terrible record.
14.5 secs: Hydro-geologist and long-time anti-nuclear activist Dr Stefan Cramer feared too many locals were not aware of Tasman’s plans and didn’t understand uranium mining. He rallied media, and local stakeholders.
DR STEFAN CRAMER, SCIENCE ADVISER, SOUTH AFRICAN FAITH COMMUNITIES’ ENVIRONMENTAL INITIATIVE: If you mine uranium in a Karoo setting, you have to drill and blast and that creates radioactive dust which travels with the strong wind many, many kilometers, sometimes hundreds of kilometers. That means the impact of uranium mining is not limited to the mine site itself, it affects many people.
JOHN LINK: Mention the word radiation and the responses are likely to vary from mild alarm to sheer and utter terror. That is the biggest challenge facing the mine’s proponents, to overcome and change that perception.
21 secs: Uranium is weakly radioactive but, crushed by mining, dissolved and exposed to oxygen, it breaks down into highly radioactive products that can enter water, soil and the food chain and remain for geological ages. Agri Eastern Cape president Doug Stern’s concern is for the Karoo’s exports.
DOUG STERN, PRESIDENT: AGRI EASTERN CAPE: These huge, big trucks come in, they get loaded with the material from the open-cast mining…Now can you imagine if that radio-active material is attached to the lanoline of our wool and mohair. What is going to happen if we try and export that wool?
20 secs: Left-over radio-active, chemically toxic sludge, called tailings, will be stored in perpetuity in a tailings dam. Similar dams in Joburg have been linked to the area’s notorious acid mine drainage problem. This prospect frightens sheep and angora goat farmer Jan Bostander, located adjacent to the mine.
JAN BOSTANDER, FARMER AND CONSERVATION COMMITTEE MEMBER: In our area, water is quite a problem. Very deep – I’m talking about 10 pipes, 11 pipes, many of us talk of 15 pipes, deep into the earth. So, it is our greatest worry, if our water will dry up completely. We have pumps that no longer supply water.
20.5 secs: In 2010 Beaufort West ran out of water. The town’s dams are only sporadically filled when rains come. In 2011, with R24-million in emergency relief funding from National Treasury, the town got South Africa’s first toilet-to-tap plant that treats wastewater effluent converting it to drinking water standard.
JOHN LINK: This water reclamation plant is symbolic of a town doing what it must in order to survive. As you’d imagine, in an environment like that, people would be willing to compromise for the greater good. But on the mining issue, the two sides are on the opposite ends of a very significant divide.
27 secs: Beaufort West’s engineers are currently trying to raise R30-million from national government for new boreholes for the town. These are planned for Quaggasfontein, an area also in Tasman’s sights. The mine says it will need more than a billion litres of water annually. Resident Callie Potgieter worries that the town’s limited water simply cannot provide for locals, farmers as well as potential fracking and mining operations.
DR CALLIE POTGIETER, DENTIST AND CONCERNED RESIDENT: At the meeting where I was, the area of Quaggasfontein was marked with these red lines and then they said, no, they’re not going to go near Quaggasfontein because it’s an environmentally sensitive area. And it’s too close to town. Quaggasfontein is now back in the mix.
5.5 secs: CEO Willie Bezuidenhout spoke to us from Joburg about this area.
JOHN WEBB: Willie, why was Quaggasfontein originally determined to be a sensitive area and now that’s no longer the case?
WILLIE BEZUIDENHOUT, CEO: TASMAN RSA MINES: Through an extensive EIA and consultation process the information that our surveys has presented to us in terms of Quaggasfontein, has illustrated some areas of sensitivity. What we are doing at the moment however is really assessing what mitigating factors you can take in Quaggasfontein.
16.5 secs: Tefo Maloisane, director of Tasman’s joint-venture partner, says a processing plant and tailings dam are planned for Rystkuil, forty kilometres outside of town. Companies like Soekor and the French Areva mined there before the uranium price tanked.
TEFO MALOISANE, DIRECTOR: TASMAN RSA MINES: We came on in 2006 and between then and now have been exploring. This area in particular was drilled out historically in the 70s. At the time, the environmental legislation did not compel cleanup. We’ve taken the approach that whilst we wait for certainty, let’s do clean-ups.
8 secs: Ecologist Sue Milton-Dean has been involved in environmental impact studies on these sites for various companies.
PROF. SUE MILTON-DEAN, ECOLOGIST: The Rystkuil area is an ephemeral wetland. That means when it rains, it becomes wet. Very wet and clay-ey for quite a long time and when you take heavy vehicles onto those clay soils, you leave permanent ruts in the ground which can be 30 cm deep. It makes it very difficult then for the natural vegetation to recover.
11 secs: At Rietkuil, another site earmarked for prospecting, radioactive waste has been left exposed by historic miners. Farm owner Christie Mocke grew up there.
CHRISTIE MOCKE, FARM OWNER: We have lived with it for a long time and no animal has ever gotten sick, and no person. There are frogs there in the hole, for 30 years already, they’ve never grown two or three heads or more legs. And at the back where the active material lies there are dassies that live in that rock and they are completely healthy.
14 secs: Like Mocke, proponents of uranium mining, including just ousted ANC mayor Truman Prince, question the validity of the naysayers’ expert views, weighing them up against economic opportunities.
TRUMAN PRINCE, BEAUFORT WEST MAYOR: We received reports that there is going to be no contamination of water and we believe in that research and we are glad to receive the uranium mine prospectation here in our area in order to give our people the much-needed jobs, which we need to boost the economy.
JOHN WEBB: 250 permanent jobs isn’t going to solve the unemployment crisis in the Karoo, let’s be frank.
TEFO MALOISANE: We’ve been very circumspect in the way we make promises. At this stage that is what we can deliver. I have yet to meet a business in Beaufort-West that employs 250 people.
21 secs: Though the proposed exploration area has now shrunk, Tasman says it aims to expand. For now it’s in the hands of national government to consider a license – and only after public consultation. Through its parent company in Australia, Tasman has buyers for its uranium but it’s bargaining on a rising price when operations begin.
WILLIE BEZUIDENHOUT, TASMAN RSA MINES CEO: We’re confident that there’s adequate and sufficient resources available to sustain mining operations for at least 20 years in Rystkuil – the other areas that we’re still targeting in terms of exploration areas, they form part of our medium to long term planning.
DR STEFAN CRAMER, SCIENCE ADVISER, SOUTH AFRICAN FAITH COMMUNITIES’ ENVIRONMENTAL INITIATIVE: We’ll see a Karoo devastated by open pit and unrehabilitated mine sites which creates a massive impact particularly on ground water flows. The impact on vegetation and therefore on agriculture is extending far beyond the mining concessions as we know them.

DR STEFAN CRAMER, SCIENCE ADVISER, SOUTH AFRICAN FAITH COMMUNITIES’ ENVIRONMENTAL INITIATIVE: We’ll see a Karoo devastated by open pit and unrehabilitated mine sites which creates a massive impact particularly on ground water flows. The impact on vegetation and therefore on agriculture is extending far beyond the mining concessions as we know them.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Despite a flatlining world uranium price, Australian miner Peninsula, backed by Russian capital, angles to mine uranium in the Karoo, threatening precious water sources.
metadata.Summary: Very nearly too late, experts and affected parties -- like the vulnerable farmers of the Karoo, heard that Peninsula Energy and its local partners have been planning to mine 750,000ha of the water-scarce, ecologically sensitive region. But by mid-year, Karoo-based Dr Stefan Cramer, science advisor to the Southern African Faith Communities' Environment Initiative (SAFCEI is taking government to court for its secretive handling of the new nuclear build programme) had rallied massive support of communities in the region to make their voices heard against the company's plans to use up and pollute major water sources in its quest for uranium profits. Now the company has pulled back on its original plan, reducing their application to only 70,000ha. What made them do this? Was the the rising tide of activism against their now slowing dawning plans? Was the the astute analysis of their ostensibly self-serving environmental impact assessments by provincial environmental departments and organised agriculture? Does the reduction in the territory make any difference to the amount of water that will be lost now and in the generations to come -- as uranium and its toxic decay products linger in the environment for geological ages to come.
metadata.Further information: Peninsula's full proposal can be viewed here: https://www.dropbox.com/s/kbd0zibgrmoch14/Update%20to%20IAP%20-%206%20July%202016.pdf?dl=0 Activists believe that it was constructive and measured criticism by the Karoo people and civil society of the pending mining rights application that forced the company to reduce its mining rights footprint to 12 % of their original intention. They believe the company pre-empted an outright rejection of the application by the Department of Mineral Resources. That is why even the vastly reduced application has to be done from scratch. While this is a victory in the short term, the fact remains that it would seem the company is working to elbow out any competition in the region by holding out promises for jobs, to position themselves for a new nuclear future in the country. Meanwhile, ahead of local government elections, the ANC mayor for Beaufort West, Truman Prince, has said that he has many plans to put the small Karoo town on the global map, including plans for fracking and large-scale uranium mining. And he totally discounted any warnings about radiological water contamination.
